article_title: Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory
citation: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5
title: Speech-memory paradigm: a short-term auditory-cognitive training with natural continuous speech and varying memory load, in audio-only and immersive stereoscopic VR modalities
description: The training element is a speech-memory task in which participants hear natural continuous sentences with varying memory loads (one vs two sentences, 60 items per session) and answer a verbal comprehension question after each item. As the article describes it, "The AU and IM approach used the same training task and consisted of a speech-memory task, whereby participants were presented with natural continuous sentences with varying memory loads and were required to answer a comprehension question after each sentence." The immersive version presents the speaker via a stereoscopic three-dimensional 180-degree video in an HP Reverb G2 head-mounted display; sessions lasted about 40-45 minutes, and comprehension questions after high-load items always referred to the first heard sentence, with mock items every tenth trial to prevent listening strategies.
requirements: Natural continuous speech material presented at a normalized 70 dB level with comprehension questions to enforce processing
Randomized item order and single presentation of each item to reduce repetition-based learning effects
constraints: The immersive environment predominantly increased redundant sensory information given the very favorable listening situation, per the authors' interpretation; perceived immersion was not systematically assessed
target_learners: healthy older adults (61-80) with mild to moderate hearing loss and varying cognitive capacities
target_learning_goals: speech comprehension of natural continuous speech
selective attention and working memory engagement during listening
examples: Each session contained 30 low-load (one-sentence) and 30 high-load (two-sentence) items on general-knowledge topics such as Flora, Fauna, and Swiss History, spoken by a trained actress who was also the visualized speaker

article_title: Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage?
citation: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y
title: The synaptic plasticity and memory (SPM) hypothesis holds that experience-dependent synaptic change is a fundamental mechanism of learning and memory retention
description: The SPM hypothesis proposes that memories are stored primarily through experience-dependent changes at synapses. The review describes how this concept gained sway after electrophysiological work revealed lasting activity-dependent synaptic changes such as LTP and LTD. Martin et al.'s four evidentiary criteria (detectability, mimicry, anterograde intervention, retrograde intervention) are presented as the framework for confirming it. The review concludes the hypothesis has strong support but lacks conclusive proof that memories reside at synapses.
requirements: Confirming the hypothesis requires evidence meeting Martin et al.'s criteria: detectability, mimicry, anterograde intervention, and retrograde intervention
constraints: The review states we are still without conclusive proof that memories reside at synapses, and non-synaptic mechanisms have emerged that are also capable of acting as memory substrates
target_learners: learners across species studied in memory research (mammals and invertebrates)
target_learning_goals: long-term memory storage and retention
examples: The review cites detectability of synaptic plasticity after many forms of learning and reversal learning inducing complementary reversal of synaptic plasticity

article_title: An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts
citation: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1
title: A taxonomy of spatial, pedagogic and agentic transitions and tensions between formal and informal learning spaces
description: The article defines three categories of transitions and tensions between timetabled and non-timetabled learning spaces. 'Spatial' ones "exist as a function of timetables and architectural divides between formal and informal space"; 'pedagogic' ones exist between teacher-centred transmission intent and student-centred intent, producing 'failed', hidden and postponed interactions; and 'agentic' ones occur between the fixed power dynamic of the lecture theatre and the more democratic adjacent informal space. The taxonomy emerged from mixed-methods analysis of occupancy data, ethnographic observation and field interviews, and conceptualises the spaces as interconnected ecological zones.
requirements: Requires mixed-methods data combining quantitative occupancy monitoring with ethnographic observation and field interviews to detect the transitions and tensions
constraints: Derived from one lecture theatre and adjacent breakout space in a UK STEM university chemical engineering department
target_learning_goals: supporting active learning
managing transitions between timetabled and non-timetabled learning
examples: Occupancy plots of type 1 and type 2 timetable configurations, sociograms of breakout space interaction, and field interviews with students were used to characterise on-ramp and off-ramp transitions

article_title: Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively
citation: Utkarsh Upadhyay, Graham Lancashire, Christoph Moser and Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez. (2021). Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively. npj Science of Learning 6:26. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00105-8
title: Spaced selection framework: optimizing question selection probabilities under an exponential forgetting curve model
description: The article introduces a machine learning modeling framework that, rather than optimizing the rate of study, optimizes which questions to include in each study session. It represents study sessions as triplets of time, question set, and recall vector, models recall probability with the "exponential forgetting curve model with binary recalls", estimates forgetting rates via a variant of half-life regression, and derives optimal selection probabilities p*_i(t) = (1/√q)(1 − m_i(t)) using stochastic optimal control. The resulting procedure is named SELECT.
requirements: Learner review and recall data to estimate forgetting rates via half-life regression
Learners must be tested in each study session, as in the app used
constraints: The parameter q trades off recall probability upon review and study-session size; in the trial the user chose session size, so results are agnostic to q
target_learners: Adult learners (18+) studying large sets of paired-associate items, e.g., driver's permit theory questions
target_learning_goals: Long-term memorization and retention of factual paired-associate content
examples: In the randomized trial, the app presented questions in the order given by the selection probability while the user chose the size of the study session.

article_title: Does splitting sleep improve long-term memory in chronically sleep deprived adolescents?
citation: Cousins, J. N., van Rijn, E., Ong, J. L., Wong, K. F., & Chee, M. W. L. (2019). Does splitting sleep improve long-term memory in chronically sleep deprived adolescents? npj Science of Learning 4:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0047-z
title: For chronically sleep-restricted learners, scheduling a daytime nap as part of a split sleep schedule can harness afternoon learning without impairing morning learning
description: This principle holds that when adolescents cannot obtain adequate nocturnal sleep, dividing the available sleep between a shortened night and a mid-afternoon nap supports memory better than concentrating the same total sleep at night, particularly for afternoon learning. The article states that "a split sleep schedule appears to be preferable for harnessing the cognitive functions that underpin learning in the afternoon, without negatively impacting upon morning learning", and that "facilitating naps in schools may be an effective measure to improve learning outcomes". It is grounded in the experimental comparison of split versus continuous restricted sleep on picture encoding and factual knowledge.
requirements: A mid-afternoon nap opportunity (1.5 h in the study, chosen to allow a full cycle of N2, SWS and REM sleep) in addition to nocturnal sleep
constraints: The evidence applies under sleep restriction below the recommended 8–10 h; whether splitting sleep advantages adolescents with adequate habitual sleep was not tested
The 90-min nap "is toward the upper limits of nap durations that may be practical to implement in schools"; shorter naps of 30–60 min have shown benefits but were not tested in this schedule
Splitting sleep reduced total sleep time and REM sleep, and REM-linked faculties (procedural memory, creative problem solving, emotional regulation) may have been affected
target_learning_goals: Long-term memory for school learning material encoded across the school day (factual knowledge and picture recognition)
examples: In the simulated school week, the split group's 1.5 h nap at 14:00–15:30 followed afternoon learning blocks about amphibian species, and the group remembered more of that material after recovery sleep

article_title: Evidence for a unitary structure of spatial cognition beyond general intelligence
citation: Malanchini, M., Rimfeld, K., Shakeshaft, N. G., McMillan, A., Schofield, K. L., Rodic, M., Rossi, V., Kovas, Y., Dale, P. S., Tucker-Drob, E. M. & Plomin, R. (2020). Evidence for a unitary structure of spatial cognition beyond general intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0067-8
title: Spatial Spy: a gamified virtual-reality battery assessing six spatial orientation skills
description: Spatial Spy is a novel gamified online battery set in a virtual city, developed in Unity by ETT Solutions, assessing six spatial orientation skills: map reading, route memory, navigation by directions, navigation by landmarks, large-scale scanning and large-scale perspective taking. Participants "solve a mystery by collecting clues while orienting and navigating around the streets of a virtual environment". Tasks combine accuracy and reaction-time scores equally weighted; the battery took 35–60 minutes (median 43) and was validated in 2,660 TEDS twins.
requirements: A web browser on a desktop or laptop computer with mouse or trackpad and keyboard; a training session and practice trials precede testing
constraints: Assessment in a computer-simulated environment may capture spatial orientation less well than real-life settings; the authors propose VR orientation may reflect an allocentric approximation of egocentric real-life orientation
target_learning_goals: spatial orientation and navigation skills (map reading, route memory, wayfinding, scanning, perspective taking)
examples: TEDS twins completed the battery online in web browsers, pausing with the 'P' key; test–retest reliability was estimated in a 100-participant pilot completing the battery twice over two months

article_title: Differences in spatiotemporal brain network dynamics of Montessori and traditionally schooled students
citation: Zanchi, P., Mullier, E., Fornari, E., Guerrier de Dumast, P., Alemán-Gómez, Y., Ledoux, J.-B., Beaty, R., Hagmann, P., & Denervaud, S. (2024). Differences in spatiotemporal brain network dynamics of Montessori and traditionally schooled students. npj Science of Learning, 9, 45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00254-6
title: The spatiotemporal connectome framework characterizes brain dynamics via system diversity (integration) and spatiotemporal diversity (stability)
description: The spatiotemporal connectome is an analytical framework that characterizes resting-state functional connectivity with a structural prior: neural activity is chunked into time windows, connectivity matrices (506 × 506 regions) constrained by structural connectivity are translated into connected components (CCs), and CCs are classified by the eight functional systems of Yeo's atlas plus the cerebellar system. From these, two group-level metrics are derived: "system diversity (SD) and spatiotemporal diversity (STD)", where SD informs about "integration and segregation" and STD about "temporal stability". The article uses these metrics to compare Montessori- and traditionally schooled students at global and functional-system scales.
requirements: SD and STD require a sufficient number of connected components for a reliable outcome, so they are computed at group level rather than individually
constraints: SD and STD are group-level measures, which prevents correlating brain metrics with individual behavioral measures in this study
target_learners: students aged 4 to 18 in Montessori or traditional schools
target_learning_goals: characterizing how pedagogical experience relates to brain network integration and temporal stability
examples: The article applied the framework to 87 students' resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI, comparing SD and STD at global and functional-system scales between pedagogy groups.

citation: Katie A. Gilligan-Lee, Zachary C. K. Hawes and Kelly S. Mix. (2022). Spatial thinking as the missing piece in mathematics curricula. npj Science of Learning 7:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00128-9
title: Spatial visualization skills taxonomy: mental rotation, mental transformation, perspective taking, and spatial scaling
description: The article organizes target spatial skills under the umbrella of spatial visualization, defined as "the ability to generate and mentally manipulate objects or images". As shown in its Fig. 1, activities targeting spatial visualization include mental rotation (mentally turning objects/shapes by degrees of rotation), mental transformation (mentally combining or deconstructing shapes within or across planes), perspective taking (imagining scenes from different points of view), and spatial scaling (mentally mapping between spaces of different scales). constraints: The article notes these activities are seldom referenced in mathematics curricula and none are mentioned in the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

using spatial visualization as a mental blackboard to model and manipulate mathematical problems and relations

description: The article recommends keeping existing shape and measurement curriculum strands and using them as entry points for spatial thinking, rather than eliminating them. citation: Alalawi, K., Athauda, R., & Chiong, R. (2024). It lets academics generate course-specific predictive models from historical continuous assessment data, run predictions after each assessment, identify at-risk students via dashboards, and deliver personalised interventions. The article states that "SPPA is implemented as a web application and is accessible by course instructors (also called academics in this paper) and students via a web browser." It integrates pedagogical principles such as constructive alignment and Hattie and Timperley's feedback model, and is released as an open-source project.

constraints: Prediction and intervention are only possible after students submit at least the first continuous assessment task

improved pass rates and grades through targeted interventions
examples: Deployed in six courses at a tertiary institution with four academics piloting learning analytics interventions

citation: Rebecka Weegar · Peter Idestam-Almquist. (2024). Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00322-1
title: Modular spreadsheet-based grading setup combining clustering, sampled manual grading, classification, and full review

title: Assess internal consistency of AI-based scores by splitting input text into comparable parts and correlating part scores
description: This principle recommends dividing the input text into two or more parts of comparable length, obtaining an AI-based score for each part, and calculating a measure of stability between the part scores as an estimate of internal consistency. target_learning_goals: reliable automated scoring of written work
examples: In the empirical example, each text was split into two parts with similar or equal numbers of sentences, and Yule's Q was calculated with analytical confidence intervals

description: The article frames the spacing effect as an explanatory account of why distributed practice improves retention, noting that "the mechanisms underlying the consolidation of long-term memory remain a topic of ongoing research, with multiple hypotheses coexisting." Per Table 1, SPSP materials included "pictures, scenarios, problem-based questions", delivered via "Gallery work, each one teaches one, group discussion, pictorial method, and simulation", with 15-minute SP interviews followed by 10-minute structured debriefing in groups of 5 to 8 students. Trained standardized patients portrayed signs and symptoms of mental illness across MSE domains, and students rotated through nurse and observer roles.

A skills laboratory with semi-cycle seating and MSE checklists for students
Trained research trainers facilitating sessions of 120 minutes, three sessions per week
constraints: The study did not show the separate effect of the lecture embedded in the SPSP training materials
SPs did not portray all symptom domains, since portraying all symptoms might exaggerate those of a real patient
target_learners: Diploma nursing students in middle college (ages 16–32)
target_learning_goals: Mental status evaluation cognition: concept, content and implementation of MSE for identifying mental illness
examples: In the study, the intervention group interviewed an SP portraying abusive language, over-talkativeness, delusions and hearing voices, while controls learned via lectures and real patients without mental illness symptoms in general medical wards

description: The article recommends that basic sciences revision continue beyond the early undergraduate years, because some early concepts may not be fully reinforced. Medical educators "should consider the use of a spiral curriculum which involves iterative revisiting of topics with each encounter building on the previous knowledge", which the authors say will enhance deep learning, reinforce prior knowledge and stimulate knowledge integration. deep learning and knowledge integration

In this study these frameworks operationalize what peer observers watch for during simulated consultations and what feedback the practising student receives.

Observer assignments distributed to the non-practising students in each group

diagnosis and treatment planning

article_title: Clinical study of skill assessment based on time sequential measurement changes.
citation: Yamaguchi Tomoko, Nakamura Ryoichi, Kuboki Akihito, Otori Nobuyoshi. (2022). Clinical study of skill assessment based on time sequential measurement changes. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-10502-7
title: Surgical process model comparison via DTW and DTW barycenter averaging as a framework for automatic detection of surgical improvement points
description: The framework quantifies surgery as a surgical process model (SPM), a time series of surgical feature parameters capturing motion and position of instruments, then aligns resident and expert SPMs with dynamic time warping (DTW), which "can align the lengths of sequences while matching similar parts so that two sequences with different lengths are best matched". Because DTW only makes one-to-one comparisons, DTW barycenter averaging (DBA) builds a standard expert model from multiple expert sequences. Comparing a resident SPM against this standard identifies portions whose average cost exceeds an empirically set threshold, automatically locating improvement points.
requirements: A standard expert SPM built from expert data, and detection conditions (average cost ≥ 8 for 6 s) empirically set to avoid detecting instantaneous movements
constraints: The comparison requires procedures whose transitions and treatment content are the same from case to case; adapting the standard SPM to individual surgical styles remains future work
target_learners: surgical residents performing endoscopic sinus surgery
target_learning_goals: improving surgical technique by locating procedure bottlenecks and improvement points
examples: The method was verified on clinical data of 39 patients, with nine experts and 19 residents participating at the Jikei University School of Medicine

article_title: The application of the spot the difference teaching method in clinical skills training for residents.
citation: Yang Liu, Li Wen, Zou Jian, An Junnan, Zeng Bin, Zheng Yitao, Yang Jiming, Ren Jia. (2022). The application of the spot the difference teaching method in clinical skills training for residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03612-3
title: Spot the difference teaching method (SDTM): a game-based observational learning model for clinical skills
description: SDTM adapts the childhood "spot the difference" game — "a prototypical change blindness task" — to clinical skills training. Teachers predesign difference points (DPs), error-prone points inserted into flawed videos matched to standard videos; trainees watch, mark deficiencies on scoring sheets, then perform and verbally correct the skill, integrating observation learning, PBL, guided learning and peer-assisted teaching. The rationale is that the game doubly activates the right posterior parietal cortex, implicated in imitation, attention and long-term memory encoding.
requirements: Reference standards, either flawless videos or a set of training criteria, are essential elements for SDTM
Difference points must be discussed and decided by the teaching group before class
constraints: PBL has situation dependencies, while SDTM does not; SDTM questions are teacher-designed with constant correct answers
The training process of comparing former and later operation videos differs from the original game
target_learning_goals: basic clinical skills such as history-taking, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, dressing change, disinfection and draping, gowning and gloving
examples: Approximately three DPs were arranged in each standard video, e.g. compression depth of approximately 0.5 inches with fingers on the chest in the CPR video

article_title: Using working memory performance to predict mathematics performance 2 years on.
citation: Allen, K., Giofrè, D., Higgins, S., & Adams, J. (2020). Using working memory performance to predict mathematics performance 2 years on. Psychological Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-020-01382-5
title: Subdivision of visuospatial working memory into spatial–simultaneous and spatial–sequential subcomponents based on encoding format
description: The article adopts and tests a subdivision of visuospatial working memory into two subcomponents defined by how information is presented at encoding. Spatial–simultaneous tasks "require participants to recall a visual array when all items are presented simultaneously", whilst spatial–sequential tasks "require recall of visual locations presented sequentially". The article cites evidence for a double dissociation between the subtypes and argues that deficits in these subcomponents could act as a specific vulnerability for mathematical difficulties, making the distinction important for predicting mathematics performance.
requirements: The distinction rests on the presentation format of stimuli during the encoding phase of the tasks used to measure each subcomponent.
constraints: The article notes the relationships between these visuospatial subcomponents and mathematics were not, as yet, thoroughly understood.
target_learning_goals: predicting and supporting mathematical performance
examples: At T1 children completed 4×3 and 4×4 dot matrix tasks (simultaneous) and 3×3 and 4×3 dot matrix and block recall tasks (sequential).

article_title: Does seniority always correlate with simulated intubation performance? Comparing endotracheal intubation performance across medical students, residents, and physicians using a high-fidelity simulator.
citation: Yau Sze-Yuen, Chang Yu-Che, Wu Meng-Yu, Liao Shu-Chen. (2021). Does seniority always correlate with simulated intubation performance? Comparing endotracheal intubation performance across medical students, residents, and physicians using a high-fidelity simulator. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0257969
title: Speed-force trade-off account of novice-expert differences in intubation
description: The authors offer a psychological interpretation of their findings: "there may have been a speed-force trade-off: novice physicians focused on precision at a slower pace, whereas senior physicians emphasized speed with conditional accuracy." Experienced physicians draw on extensive experience to "pre-program" fast, effortless intubation, accepting higher dental force because failed intubation risks life-threatening complications; novices follow learned guidance and standard procedures. Strong habit intrusions may cause experienced personnel to miss information beyond their attention.
requirements: Applies to procedural psychomotor skills performed under time pressure where force and speed trade off against each other.
constraints: The authors present this as a possible explanation ("there may have been"), not a tested mechanism; the study measured performance, not cognitive processes.
target_learning_goals: Procedural skill proficiency in emergency airway management
Balancing speed and safety in critical procedures
examples: The study's simulator data showed senior physicians applying more incisor force while juniors intubated more slowly, which the authors read through this trade-off lens.

description: A low-fidelity simulation element delivered in the first month of anesthesiology-specific PGY-2 training. A standardized one-hour group debriefing addressing professional guidelines and hospital policies

citation: Buljan Ivan, Marušić Matko, Tokalić Ružica, Viđak Marin, Peričić Tina Poklepović, Hren Darko, Marušić Ana. (2021). Cognitive levels in testing knowledge in evidence-based medicine: a cross sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02449-y
title: SPLIT instrument: a 36-item multiple-choice test assessing EBM knowledge across six cognitive levels and six EBM topics
description: The SPLIT (Six Progressive Levels in Testing) instrument consists of 36 multiple-choice items measuring EBM knowledge at six cognitive levels (Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analysing, Evaluating, Creating) across six EBM topics (Evidence-based practice, Internal validity, Clinical importance, Study design, Sources of evidence, Diagnostic studies). title: Spiral curriculum theory: vertical and horizontal integration that revisits clinical themes at increasing depth
description: The article describes the spiral curriculum as an integrated design "designed to be repetitive yet progressive" that "uses both vertical and horizontal integration". Vertical integration means students learn basic and clinical sciences in parallel throughout training (exemplified by problem-based learning), while horizontal integration combines disciplines such as anatomy, physiology, and biochemistry into interdisciplinary courses, commonly organized as body-system blocks. The spiral approach adds repeated, deepening revisiting of clinical themes, which the authors, citing Brauer et al., call "the most ideal form of integration" for enhancing trainees' knowledge base.
requirements: Content must be revisited at different time points in the curriculum with increasing detail and contextualization
constraints: Contrasted with the block system, where limited communication between instructors can create silos of compartmentalized knowledge and gaps in content
target_learning_goals: integration of basic and clinical sciences
retention of knowledge of clinical topics across the educational pipeline
examples: Within UBC's approach, basic clinical presentations follow a natural progression towards more complex patient profiles across the educational pipeline; dementia theory is addressed at the end of year two in the spiral curriculum

article_title: Specific feedback makes medical students better communicators.
citation: Engerer C, Berberat PO, Dinkel A, Rudolph B, Sattel H, Wuensch A. (2019). Specific feedback makes medical students better communicators. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1470-9
title: Design communication skills training around specific, structured, behavior-oriented feedback rather than general experience-based impressions
description: The article condenses best-practice feedback recommendations into a communication skills training variant in which "feedback was very specific and orientated on observable communication skills." Instead of general impressions, fellow students, trainers and standardized patients evaluate named key skills and add a feed-forward suggestion for improvement. The pre-post results suggest this design improves observed communication behavior, with the largest gains among low performers.
requirements: Key communication skills must be introduced and summarized (e.g., on a memory card) so that all feedback providers — fellow students, standardized patients and teachers — are trained to observe and evaluate the same skills
constraints: The evidence is within-group pre-post only; the article concludes only "tentatively" that specific feedback is superior to unspecific experience-oriented feedback, pending longitudinal multi-course research
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in their first clinical year
target_learning_goals: physician-patient communication skills, including starting consultations, structuring conversations, and handling patient emotions
examples: In the RCT, the intervention arm used the same curriculum, time and role-play setup as the control arm but replaced general impressions with synchronized 360° feedback on observable skills

description: The article describes spaced education (SE) as "a novel, evidence-based form of online education demonstrated to improve knowledge acquisition in randomized trials". Its classical protocol "involves a spacing effect and testing effect": repeated exposure over time reinforces and consolidates retention, and testing improves learner performance. This study implemented a modified version focused on the spacing effect via email reinforcement.

citation: Knol Mariska H., Dolan Conor V., Mellenbergh Gideon J., van der Maas Han L. J. (2016). Measuring the Quality of University Lectures: Development and Validation of the Instructional Skills Questionnaire (ISQ). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0149163
title: Provide professors with specific, well-timed, lecture-level student feedback to improve instructional skills
description: The article argues that end-of-term course evaluations are poor formative feedback because they are ill-timed, unspecific and unreliable for behaviour change. Feedback "should be well-timed, specific, reliable, and should facilitate realistic behavioural change". The ISQ operationalizes this by being administered immediately after a single lecture with detailed questions on seven instructional dimensions, enabling professors to assess, improve and re-assess their skills during a course.
requirements: Feedback collected immediately after a single lecture so it can inform upcoming lectures
Sufficient specific items per dimension to reflect the multidimensionality of instructional skills

target_learning_goals: improvement of professors' instructional skills
quality of subsequent lectures during a course

title: Spaced study-quiz cycle with feedback loop between self-assessment and restudy
description: The article's instructional pattern alternates a 20-minute study task with a 15-minute quiz task across weekly spaced sessions, so that quizzing generates recall accuracy data that feeds back into study. The platform displays a flashcard study priority cue based on personal recall accuracy, and the authors state "The past recall accuracy can be used as an explicit cue to guide the learning process and help managing study time." The feedback formed between quiz and study tasks further promotes spaced repetition of study and self-assessment sessions and can improve student engagement. Notebooks can reuse flashcards with existing recall accuracy data to pre-estimate background-topic recall in advanced notebooks.
requirements: Learning objects paired with open-ended questions; repeated spaced sessions; per-flashcard recall accuracy storage
constraints: Evidence comes from a single basic-science topic (Golgi Complex) in a laboratory setting with one-week intervals
target_learning_goals: retention of factual knowledge and self-directed study management
examples: Sessions s0, s1 and s2 separated by one-week intervals; study-quiz group studied 20 minutes then quizzed 15 minutes, quiz group quizzed only

title: Spiral-grating model of CD/DVD diffraction in the Fresnel (paraxial) approximation
description: The article models a CD or DVD as a spiral grating whose periodic groove profile is expanded in a Fourier series, with the substitution 2πr/r0 → 2πr/r0 - θ making the profile valid for all polar angles. Using the Fresnel paraxial approximation, the authors state: "Es conocido [16] que haciendo el cálculo de la difracción en la aproximación de Fresnel (paraxial) llegamos a una expresión para el campo". The resulting field expression predicts diffraction lines for orders n=1 and n=3 (Fig. 10) and, under polychromatic illumination, a white segment where all wavelengths overlap (Fig. 11), telling the observer where to place the eye.
requirements: The observation distance z must satisfy the validity condition relating z, diffraction order n, wavelength λ and disc radii Rmin and Rmax, with r0 always different from zero
constraints: The model is developed in the Fresnel paraxial approximation, valid for the stated condition on z; at z = 0 equation (3) is stated to be not valid
target_learning_goals: understanding the diffraction behaviour of spiral gratings such as CDs and DVDs
predicting where spectral orders and the white segment appear
examples: Figures 10 and 11 show the predicted diffraction lines for orders n=1 and n=3, and the overlapping white segment under polychromatic illumination

title: Spiraling curriculum design: multiple passes through the same concept set in variable contexts rather than linear concept addition
description: This design pattern places all target concepts on the table early and then revisits the same concept set repeatedly in shifting contexts, so understanding of one concept evolves in parallel with and supports the others. In the article's unit, "all Newtonian concepts are introduced no later than the Balloon Car activity. There are no additional concepts past this point", and "The unit is structured to make multiple passes through the same set of concepts in variable contexts, rather than continually adding new concepts in a linear sequence". This iterative structure is also what made closely spaced measurement of concept development possible in the study.
requirements: A fixed set of core concepts identified up front
Context shifts (new engines, new design challenges) that require reapplying the same concepts in ever longer reasoning chains
constraints: Early versions starting with an open design space were too large for students with limited experience, so redesign of a minimally functioning artifact proved more productive

net force
acceleration
experimental design practices
examples: Each engine design (balloon, rubber band, hybrid) required students to reapply all of Newton's laws in a new context, with Rubber Band Car introducing no new concepts but demanding longer Newtonian reasoning chains

a selection system for pupils that is established and properly implemented

preparedness for further science education

article_title: A View From Above
citation: M. Nielbock. (2017). A View From Above. AstroEDU manuscript no. astroedu1619. https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.00909
title: Spectral index framework for interpreting multispectral satellite imagery (NDVI, NDMI, MNDWI)
description: A spectral index is a number calculated from data obtained at different wavelengths that allows comparing the relative brightness of light reflected by the Earth's surface. constraints: NDVI values between 0 and 0.2 represent nearly vegetation free surfaces, while a value close to +1 hints to a high coverage of green vegetation; negative values indicate water areas
target_learning_goals: Identifying vegetation and open water from satellite data
Understanding how multispectral measurements quantify surface features
examples: Students construct an NDVI map of the Venice area and adjust the colour table so the first green flag reaches a value of 0.2

article_title: Teaching a plasma physics and engineering class at a liberal arts college using Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs)
citation: Bhavesh Ramkorun. (2026). Teaching a plasma physics and engineering class at a liberal arts college using Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00764
title: Split-semester CURE design: traditional instruction first half, authentic research investigation second half
description: The course is organized as a two-phase pattern: students first build foundational knowledge through lectures, homework, and a midterm exam, then apply it to an unanswered research question in the laboratory. The article describes a CURE as "a technique of 'inquiry-based' course development, where undergraduate students must apply course contents to critically think about an unsolved scientific problem". Students valued the sequencing, with one writing that the lecture-based first half "really helped me build off of what I had learned so that I could apply it to second half of the semester".
requirements: Access to a working research apparatus (a capacitively coupled argon plasma chamber) and diagnostics (Langmuir probe, optical emission spectrometer) that students can operate
A genuine unanswered research question connected to the course content
constraints: The article notes the educational results came from a class of only six students and should not be generalized beyond that class
target_learners: undergraduates from a wide range of scientific and engineering backgrounds at a small liberal arts college
target_learning_goals: apply fundamental plasma physics to an authentic unsolved research problem
develop laboratory, data-analysis, literature-reading, hypothesis-formulation, and science-communication skills
examples: The first half of the semester covered dusty plasmas, single-particle motion, and diagnostics via weekly topics with homework and a midterm; the second half had students collect Langmuir probe and OES data across magnetic-field strengths, analyze results, and prepare research posters

article_title: Teaching the EPR-Paradox at High School?
citation: Gesche Pospiech. (2000). Teaching the EPR–Paradox at High School ?. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0002007
title: Spin-first quantum instruction pattern: begin with a purely quantum phenomenon without classical analogue, then reach EPR and philosophical questions
description: This lesson-level pattern organizes a first course in quantum theory around spin rather than classical analogues. The article enumerates its advantages: "Spin lies at the heart of quantum theory" and explains statistics, fine structure and spectral splitting; its mathematics is simple via Pauli matrices; the uncertainty relation is explained as principal non-existence of fixed values, drastically diminishing the danger that uncertainty is perceived as measurement mistakes; and spin is central to modern experiments from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance to EPR realizations. Via the EPR–gedanken experiment it opens a short way into the philosophical points of quantum theory.
requirements: A course structure willing to postpone or omit classical themes (trajectories, wave–particle dualism)
The Pauli-matrix apparatus as the introductory mathematics
constraints: The depth of abstract structure introduced depends on the mathematical capabilities of students
target_learners: gifted or interested pupils from age 16+
target_learning_goals: understanding spin, uncertainty as non-determination, EPR entanglement and the philosophical question of reality and objectivity in nature
examples: A two-particle spin system living in a four-dimensional Hilbert space can no longer be described classically, a proof the article says is similar to the proof of the Bell inequality
key_sources: Gesche Pospiech. (2000). Teaching the EPR–Paradox at High School ?. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0002007
